title: حِكَايَةُ الْحَمَّالِ وَ الثَّلٰثِ بَنَاتِ
titleEn: The Porter and the Three Ladies
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 54–64 (continuing directly from nights-08, whose text ends as the sorceress, disguised no longer as the Sultan's captive but restored to her own errand, starts toward the enchanted pool to free the city, just as dawn cuts Shahrazad off), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the project’s own two-pass-plus-adjudication pipeline; the edition’s own OCR is unusable. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition’s — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm exactly as Macnaghten prints it. Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms and its occasional compositor’s slips, is preserved unaltered; a few genuinely obscure or corrupt-looking forms are vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes rather than silently repaired. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized automatically once this file is published, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 9 opens by finishing the Tale of the Lord of the Black Isles: the sorceress is struck down and killed, the young man's curse is fully lifted, and the Sultan brings him home to his own capital, where the young man marries the Sultan's daughter, the fisherman who first found the enchanted fish is rewarded and marries off his own children, and everyone concerned ends the frame-tale wealthy and content. The narration then turns, almost in passing ("and this is no stranger than what happened to the porter"), to a wholly new tale: the Story of the Porter and the Three Ladies. A Baghdad porter is hired by a veiled young woman and follows her on an elaborate shopping trip through the market — fruit, meat, sweets, wine and perfumes — ending at the grand door of a house kept by three beautiful sisters. Charmed by his wit, they let him stay as their "fourth" for an evening of wine, verse and company, on condition that he ask no question about what he sees. As the wine takes hold the women strip and bathe in the house's pool, and the night closes on a repeated bawdy game in which each woman in turn makes the porter name her own private parts, boxing his ears whenever his (accurate) answer isn't the fanciful name she has in mind, until dawn cuts Shahrazad off. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularized the language toward Classical Arabic here and there, so some of the original Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit. The night is frank about both violence (the sorceress's killing) and explicit sexual comedy (the genital-naming game), and is translated that way, without euphemism.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ التَّاسِعَةُ قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-tāsiʿatu qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu
sentences.l: Then when it was the ninth night, she said, 'It has reached me, O fortunate King, that...'
sentences.i: Then, when the ninth night came, she began: 'I have heard, O fortunate King, that...'

sentences.t: أَنَّ الصَّبِيَّةَ السَّاحِرَةَ لَمَّا أَخَذَتْ مِنْ مَاءِ الْبِرْكَةِ وَ تَكَلَّمَتْ عَلَيْهِ بِكَلَامٍ لَا يُفْهَمُ تَرَاقَصَتِ السَّمَكُ وَ شَالَتْ رُؤُسَهَا وَ قَامَتْ فِي الْحَالِ وَ انْفَكَّ عَنْ أَهْلِ الْمَدِينَةِ السِّحْرُ
sentences.tr: anna al-ṣabiyyata al-sāḥirata lammā akhadhat min māʾi al-birkati wa-takallamat ʿalayhi bi-kalāmin lā yufhamu tarāqaṣati al-samaku wa-shālat ruʾūsahā wa-qāmat fī al-ḥāli wa-infakka ʿan ahli al-madīnati al-siḥru
sentences.l: that when the sorceress-girl took [some] of the pool's water and spoke over it words not understood, the fish began dancing, and raised their heads, and stood up at once, and the enchantment was released from the people of the city,
sentences.i: that when the sorceress-girl drew water from the pool and spoke over it words no one could understand, the fish began to dance, lifted their heads, and rose up at once — and the spell that bound the people of the city broke,
sentences.n: The archive spells 'their heads' with only one و where classical رُؤُوس ('heads') has two; the spelling is kept as printed and read as رُؤُسَهَا.

sentences.t: وَ صَارَتِ الْمَدِينَةُ عَامِرَةً وَ الْبَيَّاعُونَ تَبِيعُ وَ تَشْتَرِي وَ صَارَ كُلُّ وَاحِدٍ فِي صِنَاعَتِهِ وَ رَجَعَتِ الْجَزَايِرُ كَمَا كَانَتْ
sentences.tr: wa-ṣārati al-madīnatu ʿāmiratan wa-al-bayyāʿūna tabīʿu wa-tashtarī wa-ṣāra kullu wāḥidin fī ṣināʿatihi wa-rajaʿati al-jazāyiru kamā kānat
sentences.l: and the city became inhabited again, and the sellers sold and bought, and every one returned to his trade, and the islands went back to how they had been.
sentences.i: The city grew busy and full of life again: the merchants bought and sold, each man returned to his craft, and the islands became again as they had been.
sentences.n: The verb after 'the sellers' (تبيع وتشتري) is left in the singular as printed, not agreeing in number with its plural subject — a Middle Arabic looseness kept as the text has it. The islands are spelled الجزاير here, without the hamza classical جزائر takes; this is the same place later called 'the Black Islands' (الجزائر السود), the young man's own kingdom.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَنَّ الصَّبِيَّةَ السَّاحِرَةَ جَاءَتْ إِلَى الْمَلِكِ فِي الْحَالِ وَ قَالَتْ لَهُ يَا حَبِيبِي نَاوِلْنِي يَدَكَ الْكَرِيمَةَ وَ قُمْ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-ṣabiyyata al-sāḥirata jāʾat ilā al-maliki fī al-ḥāli wa-qālat lahu yā ḥabībī nāwilnī yadaka al-karīmata wa-qum
sentences.l: Then the sorceress-girl came to the king at once, and said to him, 'O my beloved, hand me your noble hand, and rise.'
sentences.i: Then the sorceress-girl came at once to the king and said, 'O my darling, give me your dear hand, and rise.'
sentences.n: She still believes the king is her devoted husband and has no notion that he has already learned her secret.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْمَلِكُ بِكَلَامٍ خَفِيٍّ تَقَرَّبِي مِنِّي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-maliku bi-kalāmin khafiyyin taqarrabī minnī
sentences.l: The king said, in a hushed voice, 'Come closer to me.'
sentences.i: The king answered under his breath, 'Come nearer to me.'
sentences.n: 'Hushed speech' signals that the king is not the doting husband he plays — he is luring her within reach of his sword.

sentences.t: فَدَنَتْ حَتَّى الْتَصَقَتْ وَ الْمَلِكُ سَلَّ سَيْفَهُ فِي يَدِهِ وَ ضَرَبَهَا فِي صَدْرِهَا فَخَرَجَ السَّيْفُ يَلْمَعُ مِنْ ظَهْرِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-danat ḥattā al-taṣaqat wa-al-maliku salla sayfahu fī yadihi wa-ḍarabahā fī ṣadrihā fa-kharaja al-sayfu yalmaʿu min ẓahrihā
sentences.l: So she drew near until she was pressed close; and the king drew his sword into his hand, and struck her in her breast, so that the sword came out gleaming from her back.
sentences.i: She pressed close against him — and the king drew his sword into his grip and drove it into her breast, so the blade came out flashing from her back.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ ضَرَبَهَا شَقَّهَا نِصْفَيْنِ وَ رَمَيْهَا عَلَى الْأَرْضِ شَطْرَيْنِ
sentences.tr: thumma ḍarabahā shaqqahā niṣfayni wa-ramayhā ʿalā al-arḍi shaṭrayni
sentences.l: Then he struck her, split her into two halves, and threw her upon the ground in two pieces.
sentences.i: Then he struck her again, cleaving her in two, and cast her to the ground in two halves.
sentences.n: The archive spells 'threw her' with ي where the classical spelling of رمى plus a suffix pronoun takes ا (رَمَاهَا) — a Middle Arabic defective-verb spelling, kept and read as رَمَيْهَا.

sentences.t: وَ خَرَجَ فَوَجَدَ الشَّابَّ الْمَسْحُورَ وَاقِفًا فِي انْتِظَارِهِ فَهَنَّأَهُ بِالسَّلَامَةِ وَ قَبَّلَ يَدَهُ وَ شَكَرَهُ
sentences.tr: wa-kharaja fa-wajada al-shābba al-masḥūra wāqifan fī intiẓārihi fa-hannaʾahu bi-al-salāmati wa-qabbala yadahu wa-shakarahu
sentences.l: And he went out, and found the enchanted young man standing waiting for him; he wished him joy of his safety, and [the young man] kissed his hand and thanked him.
sentences.i: He went out and found the once-enchanted young man standing there, waiting for him. The king wished him joy of his safety, and the young man kissed his hand and thanked him.
sentences.n: The subject shifts mid-sentence: the king congratulates the young man, and then it is the young man who kisses the king's hand in gratitude.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْمَلِكُ أَنْتَ تَقْعُدُ فِي مَدِينَتِكَ أَوْ تَجِيءُ مَعِي إِلَى مَدِينَتِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-maliku anta taqʿudu fī madīnatika aw tajīʾu maʿī ilā madīnatī
sentences.l: Then the king said to him, 'Will you stay in your own city, or come with me to my city?'
sentences.i: The king asked him, 'Will you remain in your own city, or come with me to mine?'

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الشَّابُّ يَا مَلِكَ الزَّمَانِ أَ تَدْرِي مَا بَيْنَكَ وَ بَيْنَ مَدِينَتِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-shābbu yā malika al-zamāni a-tadrī mā baynaka wa-bayna madīnatika
sentences.l: The young man said, 'O King of the Age, do you know what [lies] between you and your city?'
sentences.i: The young man said, 'O King of the Age, do you know what distance lies between you and your city?'

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْمَلِكُ يَوْمَانِ وَ نِصْفٌ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-maliku yawmāni wa-niṣfun
sentences.l: The king said, 'Two days and a half.'

sentences.t: قَالَ لَهُ الشَّابُّ أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ إِنْ كُنْتَ نَائِمًا اسْتَيْقِظْ إِنَّ بَيْنَكَ وَ بَيْنَ مَدِينَتِكَ سَنَةٌ كَامِلَةٌ لِلْمُجِدِّ الْمُسَافِرِ
sentences.tr: qāla lahu al-shābbu ayyuhā al-maliku in kunta nāʾiman istayqiẓ inna baynaka wa-bayna madīnatika sanatun kāmilatun li-al-mujiddi al-musāfiri
sentences.l: The young man said to him, 'O King, if you are asleep, awaken: between you and your city is a full year, for one who travels in earnest.'
sentences.i: The young man said, 'O King, if you are dreaming, wake up — between you and your city lies a full year's journey, even for a traveler who drives himself hard.'
sentences.n: الْمُجِدّ (from أَجَدَّ / جَدَّ في السير, 'to press on, travel with all speed') describes a hard-driving traveler; even at that pace the distance is a year, which is why the king's own two-and-a-half-day crossing needs explaining.

sentences.t: وَ مَا أَتَيْتُ فِي يَوْمَيْنِ وَ نِصْفٍ إِلَّا لِأَنَّ الْمَدِينَةَ كَانَتْ مَسْحُورَةً
sentences.tr: wa-mā ataytu fī yawmayni wa-niṣfin illā li-anna al-madīnata kānat masḥūratan
sentences.l: And I did not come in two days and a half except because the city was enchanted.
sentences.i: And I made the crossing in only two and a half days for no reason but that the city lay under a spell.

sentences.t: وَأَنَا أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ لَا أُفَارِقُكَ لَحْظَةَ عَيْنٍ
sentences.tr: wa-anā ayyuhā al-maliku lā ufāriquka laḥẓata ʿaynin
sentences.l: And I, O King, will not leave you for the blink of an eye.
sentences.i: And as for me, O King, I will not leave your side even for the blink of an eye.

sentences.t: فَقَرِحَ الْمَلِكُ ثُمَّ قَالَ الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الَّذِي مَنَّ عَلَيَّ بِكَ وَأَنْتَ وَلَدِي لِأَنِّي طُولَ عُمْرِي لَمْ أُرْزَقْ وَلَدًا
sentences.tr: fa-qariḥa al-maliku thumma qāla al-ḥamdu lillāhi alladhī manna ʿalayya bika wa-anta waladī li-annī ṭūla ʿumrī lam urzaq waladan
sentences.l: Then the king rejoiced, then said, 'Praise be to God, who has favored me with you; you are my son, for in all my life I have never been granted a son.'
sentences.i: The king's heart overflowed with joy, and he said, 'Praise be to God, who has blessed me with you — you are my son, for in my whole life I was never granted one.'
sentences.n: Printed فقرح, letters for 'was wounded, afflicted' (قَرِحَ), which makes no sense beside the king's evident delight; it is read here as a compositor's slip for فَفَرِحَ, 'and he rejoiced' — one dotting away (ف for ق) from the printed word.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ تَعَانَقَا وَفَرِحَا فَرَحًا شَدِيدًا ثُمَّ مَشَيَا حَتَّى وَصَلَا إِلَى الْقَصْرِ
sentences.tr: thumma taʿānaqā wa-fariḥā faraḥan shadīdan thumma mashayā ḥattā waṣalā ilā al-qaṣri
sentences.l: Then the two embraced, and rejoiced greatly, then they walked until they reached the palace.
sentences.i: The two embraced, and rejoiced with all their hearts, then walked on until they reached the palace.

sentences.t: وَأَمَرَ الْمَلِكُ الَّذِي كَانَ مَسْحُورًا أَرْبَابَ دَوْلَتِهِ أَنْ يَتَجَهَّزُوا لِلْمَسْفَرِ وَيُهَيُّوا أَسْبَابَهُ وَجَمِيعَ مَا يَحْتَاجُ إِلَيْهِ الْحَالُ
sentences.tr: wa-amara al-maliku alladhī kāna masḥūran arbāba dawlatihi an yatajahhazū li-al-masfari wa-yuhayyū asbābahu wa-jamīʿa mā yaḥtāju ilayhi al-ḥālu
sentences.l: And the king who had been enchanted ordered the lords of his state to prepare themselves for the journey, and to make ready its provisions and all that the occasion required.
sentences.i: The once-enchanted king ordered the great men of his realm to make ready for the journey, and to gather its provisions and everything the occasion called for.
sentences.n: لِلْمَسْفَر — a noun of time/place from سَافَرَ, 'for the departure, the journey.' 'يهيوا' is printed without the hamza that classical يُهَيِّئُوا (from هَيَّأَ, 'to make ready') takes; a Middle Arabic softening of the hamza, kept as spelled and read يُهَيُّوا.

sentences.t: فَشَرَعُوا بِالتَّجْهِيزِ مُدَّةَ عَشَرَةِ أَيَّامٍ
sentences.tr: fa-sharaʿū bi-al-tajhīzi muddata ʿasharati ayyāmin
sentences.l: So they began the preparations, for a period of ten days.
sentences.i: They set about the preparations, and it took them ten full days.

sentences.t: وَخَرَجَ هُوَ وَالسُّلْطَانُ وَقَلْبُهُ مُلْتَهِبٌ عَلَى مَدِينَتِهِ كَيْفَ يَغِيبُ عَنْهَا
sentences.tr: wa-kharaja huwa wa-al-sulṭānu wa-qalbuhu multahibun ʿalā madīnatihi kayfa yaghību ʿanhā
sentences.l: Then he and the sultan set out, his heart aflame over his city — how could he be absent from it?
sentences.i: So he and the sultan set out together, though his heart burned for his own city — how could he bear to be away from it?

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُمْ سَافَرُوا وَمَعَهُ خَمْسِينَ مَمْلُوكًا وَهَدَايَا عَظِيمَةً
sentences.tr: thumma innahum sāfarū wa-maʿahu khamsīna mamlūkan wa-hadāyā ʿaẓīmatan
sentences.l: Then they journeyed, with him fifty mamluks and great gifts.
sentences.i: Then they set off, he with fifty mamluks in his train and lavish gifts.

sentences.t: وَمَا زَالُوا مُسَافِرِينَ لَيْلًا وَنَهَارًا سَنَةً كَامِلَةً وَكَتَبَ اللَّهُ لَهُمْ بِالسَّلَامَةِ حَتَّى وَصَلُوا إِلَى الْمَدِينَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-mā zālū musāfirīna laylan wa-nahāran sanatan kāmilatan wa-kataba allāhu lahum bi-al-salāmati ḥattā waṣalū ilā al-madīnati
sentences.l: And they did not cease traveling by night and day for a full year, and God decreed safety for them, until they reached the city.
sentences.i: They journeyed on, night and day, for a full year, and God granted them safe passage, until at last they reached the city.

sentences.t: وَأَرْسَلُوا أَعْلِمُوا الْوَزِيرَ بِوُصُولِ السُّلْطَانِ وَ سَلَامَتِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-arsalū aʿlimū al-wazīra bi-wuṣūli al-sulṭāni wa-salāmatihi
sentences.l: And they sent [word]: 'Inform the vizier of the sultan's arrival and his safety.'
sentences.i: They sent messengers ahead with word: 'Tell the vizier the sultan has arrived, safe and sound.'

sentences.t: فَخَرَجَ الْوَزِيرُ وَالْعَسَاكِرُ بَعْدَ مَا قَطَعُوا الْإِيَاسَ مِنَ الْمَلِكِ
sentences.tr: fa-kharaja al-wazīru wa-al-ʿasākiru baʿda mā qaṭaʿū al-iyāsa mina al-maliki
sentences.l: So the vizier and the troops went out, after they had cut off hope of the king['s return].
sentences.i: So the vizier and the troops set out to meet him, though by then they had all but given up hope of the king.

sentences.t: فَانْبَلَّ الْعَسْكَرُ وَقَبَّلُوا الْأَرْضَ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ وَهَنُّوهُ بِالسَّلَامَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-anballa al-ʿaskaru wa-qabbalū al-arḍa bayna yadayhi wa-hannūhu bi-al-salāmati
sentences.l: Then the troops came forward, and kissed the ground before him, and wished him joy of his safety.
sentences.i: The troops came forward and kissed the ground before him, wishing him joy of his safe return.
sentences.n: Printed فانبل, which matches no verb that fits the sense here; it is most likely a compositor's slip for فَأَقْبَلَ, 'came forward, advanced' (compare the correctly printed فاقبل two lines later, of the vizier) — one letter (ق for ن) from the word printed. 'وهنوه' likewise drops the hamza that classical هَنَّأُوهُ ('they congratulated him') takes, and is read هَنُّوهُ as spelled.

sentences.t: فَدَخَلَ وَجَلَسَ عَلَى الْكُرْسِيِّ
sentences.tr: fa-dakhala wa-jalasa ʿalā al-kursiyyi
sentences.l: Then he entered, and sat upon the throne.

sentences.t: فَأَقْبَلَ الْوَزِيرُ عَلَيْهِ فَأَعْلَمَهُ بِكُلِّ مَا جَرَى عَلَى الشَّابِّ
sentences.tr: fa-aqbala al-wazīru ʿalayhi fa-aʿlamahu bi-kulli mā jarā ʿalā al-shābbi
sentences.l: Then the vizier came before him, and he [the king] told him everything that had happened to the young man.
sentences.i: The vizier came before him, and the king related to him the whole story of what had happened to the young man.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ الْوَزِيرُ مَا جَرَى عَلَى الشَّابِّ هَنَّأَهُ بِالسَّلَامَةِ وَاسْتَقَرَّ الْحَالُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-wazīru mā jarā ʿalā al-shābbi hannaʾahu bi-al-salāmati wa-istaqarra al-ḥālu
sentences.l: When the vizier heard what had happened to the young man, he wished the king joy of his safety, and matters settled down.
sentences.i: When the vizier heard the whole story, he too wished the king joy of his safe return, and things settled into their ordinary course.

sentences.t: فَأَنْعَمَ السُّلْطَانُ عَلَى نَاسٍ كَثِيرٍ
sentences.tr: fa-anʿama al-sulṭānu ʿalā nāsin kathīrin
sentences.l: Then the sultan bestowed favors upon many people.
sentences.i: The sultan then showered favors upon many people.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ الْمَلِكُ لِلْوَزِيرِ عَلَيَّ بِالصَّيَّادِ الَّذِي كَانَ أَتَانَا بِالسَّمَكِ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla al-maliku li-al-wazīri ʿalayya bi-al-ṣayyādi alladhī kāna atānā bi-al-samaki
sentences.l: And the king said to the vizier, 'Bring me the fisherman who brought us the fish.'
sentences.i: The king said to the vizier, 'Fetch me the fisherman who brought us the fish.'

sentences.t: فَأُرْسِلَ إِلَى الصَّيَّادِ الَّذِي كَانَ سَبَبًا لِخَلَاصِ أَهْلِ الْمَدِينَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-ursila ilā al-ṣayyādi alladhī kāna sababan li-khalāṣi ahli al-madīnati
sentences.l: So [word] was sent to the fisherman who had been the cause of the deliverance of the people of the city.
sentences.i: So messengers were sent for the fisherman, the very cause of the whole city's deliverance.

sentences.t: فَأُحْضِرَ وَأُخْلِعَ عَلَيْهِ وَسَأَلَهُ عَنْ حَالِهِ وَهَلْ لَهُ أَوْلَادٌ فَأَخْبَرَهُ أَنَّ لَهُ بِنْتَيْنِ وَوَلَدٍ
sentences.tr: fa-uḥḍira wa-ukhliʿa ʿalayhi wa-saʾalahu ʿan ḥālihi wa-hal lahu awlādun fa-akhbarahu anna lahu bintayni wa-waladin
sentences.l: So he was brought, and a robe of honor was bestowed upon him, and [the king] asked him about his condition, and whether he had children; and he told him that he had two daughters and a son.
sentences.i: So the fisherman was brought in and invested with a robe of honor, and the king asked after him and whether he had children; he answered that he had two daughters and a son.

sentences.t: فَأَرْسَلَ الْمَلِكُ أَحْضَرَهُمْ وَتَزَوَّجَ بِبِنْتٍ
sentences.tr: fa-arsala al-maliku aḥḍarahum wa-tazawwaja bi-bintin
sentences.l: So the king sent, and had them brought, and married one daughter,
sentences.i: The king sent for them at once, and himself married one of the daughters,

sentences.t: وَأَعْطَى الشَّابَّ الْبِنْتَ الْأُخْرَى وَجَعَلَ الْوَلَدَ خَازِنْدَارَ
sentences.tr: wa-aʿṭā al-shābba al-binta al-ukhrā wa-jaʿala al-walada khāzindāra
sentences.l: and gave the young man the other daughter, and made the son treasurer.
sentences.i: gave the young man the other daughter in marriage, and made the son his treasurer.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَلَّدَ الْوَزِيرَ وَأَرْسَلَهُ سُلْطَانًا إِلَى مَدِينَةِ الشَّابِّ الَّتِي هِيَ الْجَزَايِرُ السُّودُ
sentences.tr: thumma qallada al-wazīra wa-arsalahu sulṭānan ilā madīnati al-shābbi allatī hiya al-jazāyiru al-sūdu
sentences.l: Then he invested the vizier with authority, and sent him as sultan to the young man's city, which is the Black Islands,
sentences.i: Then he invested the vizier with office and sent him off as sultan to the young man's own city, the Black Islands,

sentences.t: وَأَرْسَلَ مَعَهُ خَمْسِينَ مَمْلُوكًا الَّذِينَ جَاؤُا مَعَهُ
sentences.tr: wa-arsala maʿahu khamsīna mamlūkan alladhīna jāʾū maʿahu
sentences.l: and sent with him the fifty mamluks who had come with him,
sentences.i: sending with him the fifty mamluks who had come along in the first place,

sentences.t: وَأَعْطَاهُ مِنَ الْخِلَعِ لِسَائِرِ الْأُمَرَاءِ
sentences.tr: wa-aʿṭāhu mina al-khilaʿi li-sāʾiri al-umarāʾi
sentences.l: and gave him robes of honor for all the emirs.
sentences.i: and gave him robes of honor to distribute among all the emirs.

sentences.t: فَتَقَبَّلَ الْوَزِيرُ يَدَيْهِ وَخَرَجَ وَسَافَرَ فِي وَقْتِهِ وَسَاعَتِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-taqabbala al-wazīru yadayhi wa-kharaja wa-sāfara fī waqtihi wa-sāʿatihi
sentences.l: Then the vizier kissed his [the king's] hands, and went out, and journeyed that very hour.
sentences.i: The vizier kissed the king's hands, took his leave, and set off without delay.

sentences.t: وَاسْتَقَرَّ السُّلْطَانُ وَالشَّابُّ وَ الصَّيَّادُ قَدْ صَارَ أَغْنَى أَهْلِ زَمَانِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-istaqarra al-sulṭānu wa-al-shābbu wa-al-ṣayyādu qad ṣāra aghnā ahli zamānihi
sentences.l: And the sultan and the young man settled down, and the fisherman had become the richest man of his age,
sentences.i: The sultan and the young man settled into their lives, and the fisherman himself became the wealthiest man of his time,

sentences.t: وَأَوْلَادُهُ صَارَتْ زَوْجَاتِ الْمُلُوكِ إِلَى أَنْ أَتَاهُمُ الْمَمَاتُ
sentences.tr: wa-awlāduhu ṣārat zawjāti al-mulūki ilā an atāhumu al-mamātu
sentences.l: and his children became wives of kings, until death came to them.
sentences.i: and his children came to be wed to kings, and so they remained until death overtook them.

sentences.t: وَمَا هَذَا بِأَعْجَبَ مِمَّا جَرَى لِلْحَمَّالِ
sentences.tr: wa-mā hādhā bi-aʿjaba mimmā jarā li-al-ḥammāli
sentences.l: And this is no more wondrous than what happened to the porter.
sentences.i: And this is no stranger a tale than what happened to the porter.
sentences.n: This closing line hands the story over to the next tale in the cycle, that of the porter and the three ladies.

sentences.t: حِكَايَةُ الْحَمَّالِ وَ الثَّلْٰثِ بَنَاتِ
sentences.tr: ḥikāyatu al-ḥammāli wa-al-thalāthi banāti
sentences.l: The Story of the Porter and the Three Girls
sentences.n: This is the tale's own section heading, printed by the edition as a body line rather than a running header — it opens a new tale within Shahrazād's telling. The word for 'three' (الثلث) is spelled defectively in the archive, missing its medial alif; it is pointed here with a dagger alif (ثَلٰث) rather than silently corrected, following the edition's own spelling.

sentences.t: فَإِنَّهُ كَانَ رَجُلٌ مِنَ الْحَمَّالِينَ فِي مَدِينَةِ بَغْدَادَ وَ كَانَ عَزَبًا
sentences.tr: fa-innahu kāna rajulun mina al-ḥammālīna fī madīnati Baghdāda wa-kāna ʿazaban
sentences.l: For, there was a man among the porters, in the city of Baghdad, and he was unmarried.
sentences.i: Now there once lived, in the city of Baghdad, a porter who was a bachelor.
sentences.n: فإنه كان... is a stock formula opening a narrative episode ('now, it happened that...'); the pronoun in إنه has no real referent, a 'dummy' subject rather than literally 'he'.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَا هُوَ فِي بَعْضِ الْأَيَّامِ وَاقِفٌ فِى السُّوقِ مُنْكِيًا عَلَى قَفَصِهِ إِذْ وَقَفَتْ عَلَيْهِ اِمْرَأَةٌ مُلَفَّعَةٌ بِإِزَارٍ مَوْصِلِيٍّ بِحَرِيرٍ بَنَفَشْ مُزَرْكَشٍ بِحَاشِيَةِ قَصَبٍ وَ بِشَرِيطٍ لَاعِبٍ
sentences.tr: fa-baynā huwa fī baʿḍi al-ayyāmi wāqifun fī al-sūqi munkiyan ʿalā qafaṣihi idh waqafat ʿalayhi imraʾatun mulaffaʿatun bi-izārin mawṣiliyyin bi-ḥarīrin banafash muzarkashin bi-ḥāshiyati qaṣabin wa-bi-sharīṭin lāʿibin
sentences.l: Now, while he, on one of the days, was standing in the market, leaning on his basket, a woman stopped before him, wrapped in a Mosul mantle, of violet silk, brocaded with a border of gold-thread lace and with a fluttering ribbon.
sentences.i: Now one day, as he stood in the marketplace leaning on his basket, a woman stopped before him — wrapped in a Mosul mantle of violet silk, brocaded with a border of gold lace and a fluttering ribbon.
sentences.n: The edition prints منكيا, which matches no ordinary word for a porter's posture at his basket; it is almost certainly a slip for مُتَّكِئًا ('leaning'), the sense followed in translation, though the rasm itself is left exactly as printed. بنفش ('violet') is a Persian color-word used here directly as an adjective, without the usual Arabic nisba ending.

sentences.t: فَوَقَفَتْ وَ شَاتْ شَعْرِيَّتَهَا فَبَانَ مِنْ تَحْتِهَا عُيُونٌ سُودٌ بِهُدْبِ أَجْفَانٍ نَاعِمَةِ الْأَطْرَافِ كَامِلَةِ الْأَوْصَافِ
sentences.tr: fa-waqafat wa-shāt shaʿriyyatahā fa-bāna min taḥtihā ʿuyūnun sūdun bi-hudbi ajfānin nāʿimati al-aṭrāfi kāmilati al-awṣāfi
sentences.l: So she stood, and [she] her face-veil, and there appeared, from beneath it, black eyes, with the fringe of lids soft at the edges, perfect in description.
sentences.i: She stood there and lifted her gauze veil, and beneath it appeared black eyes with soft, fringed lids — eyes of perfect beauty.
sentences.n: شات has no meaning as printed; it is read here as a shortened or misprinted شَالَتْ, 'she lifted' (i.e. lifted her veil), which the sense of what follows requires.

sentences.t: فَالْتَفَتَتْ إِلَى الْحَمَّالِ وَ قَالَتْ بِكَلَامٍ عَذْبٍ فَصِيحٍ هَاتِ قَفَصَكَ وَاتَّبِعْنِي
sentences.tr: fa-al-taftat ilā al-ḥammāli wa-qālat bi-kalāmin ʿadhbin faṣīḥin hāti qafaṣaka wa-ittabiʿnī
sentences.l: Then she turned to the porter, and said, in sweet and eloquent speech, 'Bring your basket, and follow me.'
sentences.i: Then she turned to the porter and said, in sweet, eloquent speech, 'Take up your basket and follow me.'

sentences.t: فَمَا صَدَّقَ الْحَمَّالُ فِي الْكَلَامِ حَتَّى أَخَذَ الْقَفَصَ وَ أَسْرَعَ وَ قَالَ يَا نَهَارَ السَّعَادَةِ يَا نَهَارَ التَّوْفِيقِ وَ تَبِعَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-mā ṣaddaqa al-ḥammālu fī al-kalāmi ḥattā akhadha al-qafaṣa wa-asraʿa wa-qāla yā nahāra al-saʿādati yā nahāra al-tawfīqi wa-tabiʿahā
sentences.l: The porter had hardly believed the words when he took the basket and hurried, and said, 'O day of happiness! O day of good fortune!' and followed her.
sentences.i: The porter could scarcely believe his ears before he snatched up the basket and hurried after her, crying, 'O day of happiness! O day of good fortune!'

sentences.t: إِلَى أَنْ وَقَفَتْ عَلَى بَابِ دَارٍ فَطَرَقَتِ الْبَابَ فَنَزَلَ لَهَا رَجُلٌ نَصْرَانِيٌّ
sentences.tr: ilā an waqafat ʿalā bābi dārin fa-ṭaraqati al-bāba fa-nazala lahā rajulun naṣrāniyyun
sentences.l: until she stopped at the door of a house, and knocked at the door, and a Christian man came down to her.
sentences.i: until she stopped before the door of a house and knocked, and a Christian man came down to her.

sentences.t: فَأَعْطَتْهُ دِينَارًا وَ أَخَذَتْ مِنْهُ مَرُوقَةً زَيْتُونِيَّةً فَحَطَّتْهَا فِى الْقَفَصِ وَ قَالَتْ شِلْ وَ اتَّبِعْنِي
sentences.tr: fa-aʿṭathu dīnāran wa-akhadhat minhu marūqatan zaytūniyyatan fa-ḥaṭṭathā fī al-qafaṣi wa-qālat shil wa-ittabiʿnī
sentences.l: So she gave him a dinar, and took from him an olive-jar, and put it in the basket, and said, 'Lift it, and follow me.'
sentences.i: She paid him a dinar and took from him a jar of olives, set it in the basket, and said, 'Lift it, and follow me.'
sentences.n: مروقة is an unusual word for the vessel; it most likely names some kind of jar or flask (perhaps a colloquial or otherwise-unattested form), here holding olives bought from a Christian wine- and oil-seller, a stock detail of old Baghdad's markets. شِلْ ('lift, carry') is a colloquial imperative that recurs through this whole shopping scene, standing in for classical اِحْمِلْ.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْحَمَّالُ هٰذَا وَاللَّهِ نَهَارٌ مُبَارَكٌ وَ نَهَارٌ سَعِيدٌ بِالْقَبُولِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-ḥammālu hādhā wa-allāhi nahārun mubārakun wa-nahārun saʿīdun bi-al-qabūli
sentences.l: The porter said, 'This, by God, is a blessed day, and a fortunate day, graciously accepted!'
sentences.i: The porter said, 'This, by God, is a blessed day — a day of good fortune, and welcome indeed!'

sentences.t: فَشَالَ الْقَفَصَ وَ تَبِعَهَا فَوَقَفَتْ عَلَى دُكَّانِ فَكَهَانِيٍّ وَ اِشْتَرَتْ مِنْهُ تُفَّاحًا شَامِيًّا وَ سَفَرْجَلًا عُثْمَانِيًّا وَ خَوْخًا عَلْمَانِيًّا وَ يَاسَمِينًا وَ نُوفَرًا شَامِيًّا وَ خِيَارًا أَقْلَامِيًّا وَ لَيْمُونًا مُرَابِيًّا وَ نَارَنْجًا سُلْطَانِيًّا وَ مَرْسِينًا رَيْحَانِيًّا وَ تَمْرَحِنًا وَ أُقْحُوَانًا وَ شَقَايِقَ النُّعْمَانِ وَ بَنَفْسَجًا وَ جُلَّنَارًا وَ نَسْرِينًا
sentences.tr: fa-shāla al-qafaṣa wa-tabiʿahā fa-waqafat ʿalā dukkāni fakahāniyyin wa-ishtarat minhu tuffāḥan shāmiyyan wa-safarjalan ʿuthmāniyyan wa-khawkhan ʿalmāniyyan wa-yāsamīnan wa-nūfaran shāmiyyan wa-khiyāran aqlāmiyyan wa-laymūnan murābiyyan wa-nāranjan sulṭāniyyan wa-marsīnan rayḥāniyyan wa-tamraḥinan wa-uqḥuwānan wa-shaqāyiqa al-nuʿmāni wa-banafsajan wa-jullanāran wa-nasrīnan
sentences.l: So he lifted the basket and followed her; and she stopped at a fruit-seller's shop, and bought from him: Damascene apples, and Ottoman quinces, and [ʿalmānī] peaches, and jasmine, and Damascene water-lilies, and pen-slender cucumbers, and candied lemons, and royal bitter-oranges, and fragrant myrtle, and henna-blossom, and chamomile, and anemones, and violets, and pomegranate-blossom, and eglantine.
sentences.i: He shouldered the basket and followed her to a fruiterer's stall, where she bought Damascene apples, Ottoman quinces, peaches, jasmine, water-lilies of Damascus, slender cucumbers, candied lemons, royal oranges, fragrant myrtle, henna-blossoms, chamomile, anemones, violets, pomegranate-flowers, and eglantine, until the basket was heaped with color and scent.
sentences.n: Each item in this catalogue is paired with its own place-name or quality epithet, a rhetorical flourish typical of the Nights' shopping-list scenes. عَلْمَانِيًّا, describing the peaches, is unexpected; it may be a misprint for عُمَانِيًّا ('Omani'), but is kept and read as printed.

sentences.t: وَ حَطَّتِ الْجَمِيعَ فِي قَفَصِ الْحَمَّالِ وَ قَالَتْ شِلْ فَشَالَ وَ تَبِعَهَا فَوَقَفَتْ عَلَى الْجَزَّارِ وَ قَالَتْ لَهُ اقْطَعْ عَشَرَةَ أَرْطَالٍ لَحْمٍ فَقَطَعَ لَهَا وَ أَعْطَتْهُ الثَّمَنَ
sentences.tr: wa-ḥaṭṭati al-jamīʿa fī qafaṣi al-ḥammāli wa-qālat shil fa-shāla wa-tabiʿahā fa-waqafat ʿalā al-jazzāri wa-qālat lahu iqṭaʿ ʿasharata arṭālin laḥmin fa-qaṭaʿa lahā wa-aʿṭathu al-thamana
sentences.l: And she put all of it in the porter's basket, and said, 'Lift it.' So he lifted it and followed her; and she stopped at the butcher's, and said to him, 'Cut ten pounds of meat.' So he cut it for her, and she gave him the price.
sentences.i: She loaded it all into the porter's basket and said, 'Lift it!' So he shouldered it and followed her to the butcher's, where she said, 'Cut me ten pounds of meat.' He cut it for her, and she paid him.

sentences.t: وَلَفَّتْهُ فِي قِرْطَاسِ مَوْزٍ وَ جَعَلَتْهُ فِي الْقَفَصِ وَ قَالَتْ شِلْ يَا حَمَّالُ فَشَالَ وَ تَبِعَهَا
sentences.tr: wa-laffathu fī qirṭāsi mawzin wa-jaʿalathu fī al-qafaṣi wa-qālat shil yā ḥammālu fa-shāla wa-tabiʿahā
sentences.l: And she wrapped it in a banana-leaf wrapper, and put it in the basket, and said, 'Lift it, O porter.' So he lifted it and followed her.
sentences.i: She wrapped it in a banana-leaf and set it in the basket, saying, 'Lift it, porter!' So he lifted it and followed her on.

sentences.t: فَأَتَتِ الصَّبِيَّةُ وَ وَقَفَتْ عَلَى النَّقْلِيِّ وَ أَخَذَتْ مِنْهُ قَلْبَ فُسْتُقٍ مَا يَصْلُحُ لِلْمِنْقَلِ وَ زَبِيبٍ تِهَامِيٍّ وَ قَلْبَ لَوْزٍ
sentences.tr: fa-atati al-ṣabiyyatu wa-waqafat ʿalā al-naqliyyi wa-akhadhat minhu qalba fustuqin mā yaṣluḥu li-al-minqali wa-zabībin tihāmiyyin wa-qalba lawzin
sentences.l: And the girl went on, and stopped at the nut-seller's, and took from him shelled pistachios such as suit the roasting-pan, and Tihama raisins, and shelled almonds.
sentences.i: The girl went on to the nut-seller's, and bought shelled pistachios fit for roasting, raisins of Tihama, and shelled almonds.

sentences.t: وَ قَالَتْ لِلْحَمَّالِ شِلْ وَ اتَّبِعْنِي فَشَالَ الْقَفَصَ وَ تَبِعَهَا إِلَى أَنْ وَقَفَتْ عَلَى دُكَّانِ الْحَلْوَانِيِّ وَ اِشْتَرَتْ طَبَقًا وَ عَبَّتْ فِيهِ مِنْ جَمِيعِ مَا عِنْدَهُ مِنْ مُشَبَّكٍ وَ قَطَايِفَ
sentences.tr: wa-qālat li-al-ḥammāli shil wa-ittabiʿnī fa-shāla al-qafaṣa wa-tabiʿahā ilā an waqafat ʿalā dukkāni al-ḥalwāniyyi wa-ishtarat ṭabaqan wa-ʿabbat fīhi min jamīʿi mā ʿindahu min mushabbakin wa-qaṭāyifa
sentences.l: And she said to the porter, 'Lift it, and follow me.' So he lifted the basket and followed her, until she stopped at the confectioner's shop, and bought a tray, and heaped onto it, from all he had: mushabbak, and qaṭāyif,
sentences.i: 'Lift it and follow me,' she told the porter; so he carried the basket after her until she stopped at the sweet-seller's, bought a tray, and piled it high with all he had — fried mushabbak, stuffed qatayif,

sentences.t: بَانِيسَكَ مَحْشِيَّةٍ وَصَابُونِيَّةٍ وَأَقْرَاصٍ لَيْمُونِيَّهْ وَمَيْمُونِيَّهْ وَأَمْشَاطِ زَيْنَبَ وَأَصَابِعَ وَلُقَيْمَاتِ الْقَاضِي
sentences.tr: bāniyusaka maḥshiyyatin wa-ṣābūniyyatin wa-aqrāṣin laymūniyyah wa-maymūniyyah wa-amshāṭi Zaynaba wa-aṣābiʿa wa-luqaymāti al-qāḍī
sentences.l: stuffed bāniyusak, and ṣābūniyya, and lemon-discs, and maymūniyya, and Zaynab's-combs, and 'fingers', and the qāḍī's little morsels,
sentences.i: stuffed bāniyusak pastries, soap-shaped sābūniyya sweets, lemon rounds, maymūniyya, 'Zaynab's combs', 'lady's fingers', and the qadi's tidbits,
sentences.n: These are all names of sweetmeats sold by weight from the confectioner's tray; several (bāniyusak, sābūniyya, 'Zaynab's combs', 'the qāḍī's morsels') are playful shape- or person-based names rather than literal descriptions, as is still true of Arab confectionery today. Two of them (ليمونيه، ميمونيه) are printed with a final ه where the rest of the list has ة; the spelling is kept as printed.

sentences.t: وَأَخَذَتْ مِنْ جَمِيعِ أَصْنَافِ الْحَلَاوَةِ فِي طَبَقٍ وَحَطَّتْهُ فِي الْقَفَصِ
sentences.tr: wa-akhadhat min jamīʿi aṣnāfi al-ḥalāwati fī ṭabaqin wa-ḥaṭṭathu fī al-qafaṣi
sentences.l: and she took, of every kind of sweet, a trayful, and put it in the basket.
sentences.i: and she took a trayful of every kind of sweet there was, and set it in the basket.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا الْحَمَّالُ كُنْتِي أَعْلِمِينِي لَأَتَيْتُ مَعِي الْكَرِيشَ تَحْمِلُ عَلَيْهِ هٰذِهِ الْخُوشْكَاتِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā al-ḥammālu kunti aʿlimīnī la-ataytu maʿī al-karīsha taḥmilu ʿalayhi hādhihi al-khushkāti
sentences.l: Then the porter said to her, 'You were — inform me! — I would have brought with me the pack-beast, to carry upon it these dainties.'
sentences.i: The porter said to her, 'Had you only told me, I would have brought along the pack-mule, to carry all these sundries.'
sentences.n: كنتِ أعلميني follows a colloquial conditional pattern of Middle/dialectal Arabic — a counterfactual 'had you told me' built without the classical لو — rather than a plain sequence of two separate statements. الكريش (literally close to 'the paunch, the big-bellied one') is used here as a nickname for a pack-animal; الخوشكات is likewise a colloquial term, here rendered loosely as 'dainties, sundries' for the mounting pile of purchases.

sentences.t: فَتَبَسَّمَتْ وَضَرَبَتْ بِيَدِهَا عَلَى قَفَاهُ وَقَالَتْ لَهُ أَسْرِعْ فِي مَشْيِكَ وَخَلِّ عَنْكَ الْكَلَامَ الْكَثِيرَ وَأَجْرُكَ حَاصِلٌ إِنْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى
sentences.tr: fa-tabassamat wa-ḍarabat bi-yadihā ʿalā qafāhu wa-qālat lahu asriʿ fī mashyika wa-khalli ʿanka al-kalāma al-kathīra wa-ajruka ḥāṣilun in shāʾa allāhu taʿālā
sentences.l: So she smiled, and struck with her hand upon the back of his neck, and said to him, 'Hurry in your walking, and leave off you so much talk; your wage is assured, if God, exalted, wills.'
sentences.i: She smiled, gave him a light cuff on the back of the neck, and said, 'Step lively, and spare me all this talk — your wage is assured, God willing.'

sentences.t: ثُمَّ وَقَفَتْ عَلَى الْعَطَّارِ وَأَخَذَتْ مِنْهُ عَشَرَةَ أَمْوَاهٍ مَاءَ وَرْدٍ وَمَاءَ زَهْرٍ وَمَاءَ نُوفَرٍ وَمَاءَ خِلَافٍ
sentences.tr: thumma waqafat ʿalā al-ʿaṭṭāri wa-akhadhat minhu ʿasharata amwāhin māʾa wardin wa-māʾa zahrin wa-māʾa nūfarin wa-māʾa khilāfin
sentences.l: Then she stopped at the perfumer's, and took from him ten waters: rose-water, and orange-blossom water, and water-lily water, and willow-flower water,
sentences.i: Then she stopped at the perfumer's and bought ten kinds of scented water from him — rose-water, orange-blossom water, water-lily water, and willow-flower water,

sentences.t: وَأَخَذَتْ أَبْلُوجَيْنِ سُكَّرٍ وَأَخَذَتْ قِزِّيزَ مَاءِ وَرْدٍ مُمَسَّكٍ وَحَصًا لُبَانٍ ذَكَرٍ وَعُودًا وَعَنْبَرًا وَمِسْكًا
sentences.tr: wa-akhadhat ablūjayni sukkarin wa-akhadhat qizzīza māʾi wardin mumassakin wa-ḥaṣan lubānin dhakarin wa-ʿūdan wa-ʿanbaran wa-miskan
sentences.l: and she took two loaves of sugar, and took a small flask of musk-scented rose-water, and pebbles of male frankincense, and aloeswood, and ambergris, and musk,
sentences.i: and bought two sugar-loaves, a small flask of musk-scented rose-water, grains of choice frankincense, aloeswood, ambergris, and musk,
sentences.n: أَبْلُوجَيْنِ (loaves of refined sugar) and قِزِّيز (a small flask or jar) are both loanwords for market goods rather than native Arabic formations; their exact shapes and sizes are not otherwise specified in the text.

sentences.t: وَأَخَذَتْ شَمْعًا إِسْكَنْدَرَانِيًّا وَحَطَّتِ الْجَمِيعَ فِى الْقَفَصِ وَ قَالَتْ شِلْ قَفَصَكَ وَاتَّبِعْنِي فَشَالَ الْقَفَصَ وَتَبِعَهَا بِهِ إِلَى أَنْ أَتَتْ إِلَى دَارٍ مَلِيحَةٍ
sentences.tr: wa-akhadhat shamʿan iskandarāniyyan wa-ḥaṭṭati al-jamīʿa fī al-qafaṣi wa-qālat shil qafaṣaka wa-ittabiʿnī fa-shāla al-qafaṣa wa-tabiʿahā bihi ilā an atat ilā dārin malīḥatin
sentences.l: and she bought Alexandrian wax, and put it all in the basket, and said, 'Lift your basket, and follow me.' So he lifted the basket and followed her with it, until she came to a beautiful house,
sentences.i: and bought Alexandrian wax candles, put it all into the basket, and said, 'Lift your basket and follow me.' So he shouldered it and followed her until she came to a fine house,

sentences.t: وَقُدَّامَهَا رَحْبَةٌ فَسِيحَةٌ عَالِيَةُ الْبُنْيَانِ مُشَيَّدَةُ الْأَرْكَانِ بَابُهَا بِدَرْقَتَيْنِ مِنَ الْأَبَنُوسِ مُصَفَّحٌ بِصَفَائِحِ الذَّهَبِ الْأَحْمَرِ
sentences.tr: wa-quddāmahā raḥbatun fasīḥatun ʿāliyatu al-bunyāni mushayyadatu al-arkāni bābuhā bi-darqatayni mina al-abanūsi muṣaffaḥun bi-ṣafāʾiḥi al-dhahabi al-aḥmari
sentences.l: and before it a spacious open court, lofty of construction, firmly-built of corners; its door had two panels of ebony, plated with sheets of red gold,
sentences.i: before it lay a broad, open forecourt, its walls rising high and solidly built; its door was made of two ebony panels, plated with sheets of red gold,

sentences.t: فَوَقَفَتِ الصَّبِيَّةُ عَلَى الْبَابِ وَأَدَارَتِ النِّقَابَ عَنْ وَجْهِهَا وَدَقَّتْ دَقًّا لَطِيفًا
sentences.tr: fa-waqafati al-ṣabiyyatu ʿalā al-bābi wa-adārati al-niqāba ʿan wajhihā wa-daqqat daqqan laṭīfan
sentences.l: So the girl stopped at the door, and turned back the veil from her face, and knocked a gentle knock,
sentences.i: The girl stood at the door, drew the veil back from her face, and gave a gentle knock,

sentences.t: وَالْحَمَّالُ وَاقِفٌ وَرَاءَهَا وَهُوَ لَمْ يَزَلْ يَتَفَكَّرُ فِي حُسْنِهَا وَجَمَالِهَا
sentences.tr: wa-al-ḥammālu wāqifun warāʾahā wa-huwa lam yazal yatafakkaru fī ḥusnihā wa-jamālihā
sentences.l: while the porter stood behind her, and he did not cease pondering her beauty and her loveliness,
sentences.i: while the porter stood behind her, still lost in thought over her beauty and loveliness.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا بِالْبَابِ قَدِ انْفَتَحَ وَتَشَرَّعَتِ الدَّرْقَتَيْنِ فَنَظَرَ الْحَمَّالُ إِلَى مَنْ فَتَحَ لَهَا الْبَابَ
sentences.tr: wa-idhā bi-al-bābi qadi infataḥa wa-tasharraʿati al-darqatayni fa-naẓara al-ḥammālu ilā man fataḥa lahā al-bāba
sentences.l: when, behold, the door had opened, and the two panels swung wide, and the porter looked at who had opened the door for her —
sentences.i: when, all at once, the door swung open, its two panels thrown wide, and the porter looked to see who had opened it for her —
sentences.n: الدرقتين is printed in the oblique form (as if object or genitive) though it is here the subject of تشرعت; this loose case-marking, common in the edition's Middle Arabic, is kept as printed.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا بِهَا خُمَاسِيَّةُ الْقَدِّ بَارِزَةُ النَّهْدِ ذَاتُ حُسْنٍ وَجَمَالٍ وَبَهَاءٍ وَكَمَالٍ وَ قَدٍّ وَاعْتِدَالٍ
sentences.tr: wa-idhā bihā khumāsiyyatu al-qaddi bārizatu al-nahdi dhātu ḥusnin wa-jamālin wa-bahāʾin wa-kamālin wa-qaddin wa-iʿtidālin
sentences.l: and behold, she was one of well-proportioned stature, prominent of bosom, possessed of beauty and loveliness and splendor and perfection, of figure and symmetry,
sentences.i: and there she stood — a girl of perfect, medium-tall figure, full-bosomed, possessed of beauty, loveliness, splendor and perfection, of fine form and symmetry,
sentences.n: خماسية القد ('of five-span stature') is a stock formula of ideal beauty in the Nights, describing a figure neither too tall nor too short.

sentences.t: بِجَبِينٍ أَزْهَرَ وَخَدٍّ أَحْمَرَ وَعُيُونٍ تُحَاكِي الْمَهَا وَالْغِزْلَانَ وَحَوَاجِبَ مِثْلَ قَوْسِ هِلَالِ شَعْبَانَ
sentences.tr: bi-jabīnin azhara wa-khaddin aḥmara wa-ʿuyūnin tuḥākī al-mahā wa-al-ghizlāna wa-ḥawājiba mithla qawsi hilāli Shaʿbāna
sentences.l: with a radiant brow, and a red cheek, and eyes that rival the wild oryx and the gazelles, and eyebrows like the bow of the crescent-moon of Shaʿbān,
sentences.i: with a radiant brow, a blushing cheek, eyes that rivalled the wild oryx and the gazelle, and eyebrows curved like the crescent moon of Shaʿbān,

sentences.t: وَخُدُودٍ مِثْلَ شَقَايِقَ النُّعْمَانِ وَ فَمٍ كَخَاتَمِ سُلَيْمَانَ وَشُفَيْهَاتٍ حُمْرٍ كَالْمَرْجَانِ وَسُنَيْنَاتٍ كَاللُّؤْلُؤِ الْمُنَضَّدِ وَالْأُقْحُوَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-khudūdin mithla shaqāyiqa al-nuʿmāni wa-famin ka-khātami Sulaymāna wa-shufayhātin ḥumrin ka-al-marjāni wa-sunaynātin ka-al-luʾluʾi al-munaḍḍadi wa-al-uqḥuwāni
sentences.l: and cheeks like anemones, and a mouth like Solomon's seal-ring, and little red lips like coral, and little teeth like well-strung pearls and chamomile,
sentences.i: cheeks like anemone-blossoms, a mouth like Solomon's own seal, small red lips like coral, and small white teeth like well-ranged pearls and chamomile-petals,

sentences.t: وَعُنُقٍ كَأَنَّهُ لِلْغِزْلَانِ وَصَدْرٍ كَأَنَّهُ شَاذَرْوَانٌ وَنَهْدَيْنِ كَأَنَّهُمَا فِحْلَيْ رُمَّانٍ
sentences.tr: wa-ʿunuqin ka-annahu li-al-ghizlāni wa-ṣadrin ka-annahu shādharwānun wa-nahdayni ka-annahumā fiḥlay rummānin
sentences.l: and a neck as though it belonged to the gazelles, and a breast as though it were a marble fountain-basin, and two breasts as though they were two pomegranate-halves,
sentences.i: a neck as graceful as a gazelle's, a bosom as smooth as a marble fountain-basin, and two breasts like twin pomegranates,
sentences.n: فحلي رمان is printed where the stock Nights image is فِلْقَتَا رُمَّانٍ ('two halves of a pomegranate'); it is very likely a compositor's misordering of those letters, but is kept and read as printed, with the same sense understood.

sentences.t: وَبَطْنٍ مُلَبَّجٍ وَسُرَّةٍ تَسَعُ أُوقِيَّةً مِنْ دُهْنِ الْبَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-baṭnin mulabbajin wa-surratin tasaʿu ūqiyyatan min duhni al-bāni
sentences.l: and a belly softly folded, and a navel holding nine ounces of ban-tree oil,
sentences.i: a softly rounded belly, and a navel deep enough to hold nine ounces of ben-oil —
sentences.n: ملبج is an uncertain word, tentatively 'softly folded, rounded'; the navel-holding-oil image is a stock hyperbole of Nights beauty-description, not to be read literally.

sentences.t: كَمَا قَالَ فِيهَا الشَّاعِرُ
sentences.tr: ka-mā qāla fīhā al-shāʿiru
sentences.l: as the poet said of her:
sentences.i: as the poet said, describing her:

sentences.t:
اُنْظُرْ إِلَى شمسِ القصورِ وبدرِها * وَ إِلَى خزامتِها وبهجةِ زهرِها
لَمْ تلقَ عينُك ابيضاً فِي اسودَ * جمعَ الجمالِ لونَها مَعَ شعرِها
محمرّةُ الوجناتِ يخبرُ حسنُها * عَنْ اسمِها إِنْ لَمْ يحظَ بخبرِها
وَ تَمَايَلَتْ فَضَحِكَتْ مِنْ اردافِها * عجباً وَلٰكِنِّي بكيتُ لخصرِها
sentences.tr:
unẓur ilā shamsi al-quṣūri wa-badri-hā * wa ilā khizāmati-hā wa-bahjati zahri-hā
lam talqa ʿaynuka abyaḍan fī aswada * jamʿa al-jamāli lawna-hā maʿa shaʿri-hā
muḥmarratu al-wajanāti yukhbiru ḥusnu-hā * ʿan ismi-hā in lam yaḥẓa bi-khabari-hā
wa tamāyalat fa-ḍaḥikat min ardāfi-hā * ʿajaban wa-lākinnī bakaytu li-khaṣri-hā
sentences.l:
Look at the sun of the palaces and her full moon, * and at her fragrance and the splendor of her blossom.
Your eye has never met white in black, * gathering all beauty, her color together with her hair.
Red of cheek — her beauty tells * of her name, if he has not had the fortune of news of her.
And she swayed, and laughed out of her hips, * in wonder — but I, I wept for her waist.
sentences.i:
Look upon the sun of the palace halls and her full moon, and upon her fragrance and the glory of her bloom.
Your eye has never seen white set against black as she does — all beauty gathered, her color together with her hair.
Rosy of cheek: her beauty alone would proclaim her name, even to one who never heard tell of her.
She swayed and laughed for wonder at her own hips — but I, for her waist, wept.
sentences.n: The last hemistich turns on a stock erotic contrast in Arabic love-poetry between the beloved's full hips and her slender waist, which supposedly cannot bear their weight; the poet weeps for the waist while the figure herself laughs at her hips.

sentences.t: قَٰلَ فَلَمَّا نَظَرَ الْحَمَّالُ إِلَيْهَا سَلَبَ عَقْلَهُ وَلُبَّهُ وَكَادَ الْقَفَصُ أَنْ يَقَعَ مِنْ عَلَى رَأْسِهِ
sentences.tr: qāla fa-lammā naẓara al-ḥammālu ilayhā salaba ʿaqlahu wa-lubbahu wa-kāda al-qafaṣu an yaqaʿa min ʿalā ra'sihi
sentences.l: He said: When the porter looked at her, it stole away his mind and his wits, and the basket nearly fell from off his head.
sentences.i: He said: When the porter looked at her, she stole away his mind and his wits, and the basket very nearly toppled from atop his head.
sentences.n: The edition prints قل here for قال ('he said'), the narrator's formula resuming the tale after a verse insertion; the missing long alif is a routine defective spelling, not an error, and is pointed here with a dagger alif rather than written out.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَ مَا رَأَيْتُ عُمْرِي أَبْرَكَ مِنْ هَٰذَا النَّهَارِ
sentences.tr: thumma qāla mā ra'aytu ʿumrī abraka min hādhā al-nahāri
sentences.l: Then he said, 'I have not seen, in my life, [anything] more blessed than this day.'
sentences.i: Then he said, 'Never in my life have I seen a more blessed day than this.'

sentences.t: فَقَالَتِ الصَّبِيَّةُ الْبَوَّابَةُ الشُّوَشْكَاشَةُ ادْخُلِي مِنَ الْبَابِ وَحُطِّي عَنْ هَٰذَا الْحَمَّالِ الْمِسْكِينِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālati al-ṣabiyyatu al-bawwābatu al-shūshkāshatu udkhulī mina al-bābi wa-ḥuṭṭī ʿan hādhā al-ḥammāli al-miskīni
sentences.l: Then the girl, the doorkeeper, [said to] the marketing-girl: 'Enter by the door, and take [the load] down from this poor porter.'
sentences.i: Then the doorkeeper-girl said to the marketing-girl, 'Go in by the door, and unload this poor porter.'
sentences.n: البوابة ('the doorkeeper') and الشوشكاشة (a household marketing-girl, an obscure loanword for a servant who does the shopping) are two of the three sisters; the address to her carries no vocative particle, an ellipsis typical of this text's narration.

sentences.t: فَدَخَلَتِ الشُّوَشْكَاشَةُ وَ وَرَاءَهَا الْبَوَّابَةُ وَالْحَمَّالُ وَمَشَوْا حَتَّى اِنْتَهَوْا إِلَى قَاعَةٍ فَسِيحَةٍ مُهَنْدَسِيَّةٍ مَاحِيَةٍ
sentences.tr: fa-dakhalati al-shūshkāshatu wa-warā'ahā al-bawwābatu wa-al-ḥammālu wa-mashaw ḥattā intahaw ilā qāʿatin fasīḥatin muhandasiyyatin māḥiyatin
sentences.l: So the marketing-girl entered, and behind her the doorkeeper and the porter, and they walked until they arrived at a spacious hall, well-engineered, whitewashed,
sentences.i: So the marketing-girl went in, with the doorkeeper and the porter behind her, and they walked on until they came to a spacious hall, finely built and freshly whitewashed,

sentences.t: ذَاتِ تَرَاكِيبَ وَ عُقُودَاتٍ وَ سَدَلَاتٍ وَ خَرَسَانَاتٍ وَ خَزَائِنَ عَلَيْهَا سُتُورٌ مُرْخِيَاتٌ وَ فِي وَسَطِ الْقَاعَهِ بِرْكَةٌ كَبِيرَةٌ مَلَانَةٌ مَاءًا وَ فِيهَا شَخْتُورٌ
sentences.tr: dhāti tarākība wa-ʿuqūdātin wa-sadalātin wa-kharasānātin wa-khazā'ina ʿalayhā sutūrun murkhiyātun wa-fī wasaṭi al-qāʿati birkatun kabīratun malānatun mā'an wa-fīhā shakhtūrun
sentences.l: having fittings, and arches, and drapings, and [stonework platforms?], and cupboards over which were let-down curtains; and in the middle of the hall a large pool, full of water, and in it a skiff,
sentences.i: furnished with paneled fittings, arches, hanging drapes, and stone-built platforms, and curtained cupboards; and in the middle of the hall a great pool brimming with water, with a little skiff upon it,
sentences.n: خرسانات is an obscure furnishing-term here rendered tentatively as raised stone platforms or daises; شختور is a loanword for a small boat or skiff. ملانة ('full') is a Middle-Arabic form of the Classical مليئة/ملأى, kept as printed.

sentences.t: وَ فِي صَدْرِ الْقَاعَةِ سَرِيرٌ مِنَ الْعَرْعَرِ مُرَصَّعٌ بِالْجَوْهَرِ مُرْخِي عَلَيْهِ نَامُوسِيَّةُ أَطْلَسٍ أَحْمَرَ أَزْرَارُهَا لُؤْلُؤٌ قَدْرَ الْبُنْدُقِ وَ أَكْبَرَ
sentences.tr: wa-fī ṣadri al-qāʿati sarīrun mina al-ʿarʿari muraṣṣaʿun bi-al-jawhari murkhī ʿalayhi nāmūsiyyatu aṭlasin aḥmara azrāruhā lu'lu'un qadra al-bunduqi wa-akbara
sentences.l: and at the head of the hall a couch of juniper-wood, studded with jewels, hung over it a mosquito-net of red satin, its buttons pearls the size of hazelnuts, and larger,
sentences.i: and at the head of the hall stood a couch of juniper-wood inlaid with gems, draped with a canopy of red satin whose toggles were pearls the size of hazelnuts, and larger,

sentences.t: وَ بَرَزَتْ مِنْ دَاخِلِهَا صَبِيَّةٌ بِطَلْعَةٍ مُضِيَّةٍ وَ بَهْجَةٍ رَضِيَّةٍ وَ أَخْلَاقٍ فَيْلَسُوفِيَّةٍ بِخِلْقَةٍ قَمَرِيَّةٍ
sentences.tr: wa-barazat min dākhilihā ṣabiyyatun bi-ṭalʿatin muḍiyyatin wa-bahjatin raḍiyyatin wa-akhlāqin faylasūfiyyatin bi-khilqatin qamariyyatin
sentences.l: and there came forth from within it a girl, with a radiant appearance and a pleasing splendor, and philosophic manners, with a moon-like form,
sentences.i: and from within it there came forth a girl of radiant countenance and serene splendor, of philosophic bearing and moonlike form,
sentences.n: 'Philosophic manners' is an unusual epithet to find amid an otherwise purely physical catalogue of beauty; the text is followed as printed.

sentences.t: وَ عُيُونٍ بَابِلِيَّةٍ وَ قِسِيِّ حَوَاجِبَ مَحْنِيَّةٍ وَ قَامَةٍ أَلِفِيَّةٍ وَ نَكْهَتٍ عَنْبَرِيَّةٍ وَ شُفَيْفَاتٍ عَقِيقِيَّةٍ سُكَّرِيَّةٍ وَ وَجْهٍ يُخْجِلُ نُورُهُ الشَّمْسَ الْمُضِيَّةَ
sentences.tr: wa-ʿuyūnin bābiliyyatin wa-qisiyyi ḥawājiba maḥniyyatin wa-qāmatin alifiyyatin wa-nakhatin ʿanbariyyatin wa-shufayfātin ʿaqīqiyyatin sukkariyyatin wa-wajhin yukhjilu nūruhu al-shamsa al-muḍī'ata
sentences.l: and Babylonian eyes, and bows of eyebrows, arched, and a stature like the letter alif, and a breath of ambergris, and little lips of sugared carnelian, and a face whose light puts to shame the radiant sun,
sentences.i: and eyes as bewitching as Babylon's, brows arched like bows, a figure straight as the letter alif, an ambergris-scented breath, sweet carnelian lips, and a face whose light shamed the radiant sun,
sentences.n: 'Babylonian eyes' alludes to Babylon's association with sorcery (cf. the angels Hārūt and Mārūt, who according to the Qur'an taught magic there) — bewitching eyes. نكهت is printed with ت rather than the expected ة of نكهة ('scent, breath'); kept as printed.

sentences.t: وَ هِيَ كَأَنَّهَا بَعْضُ الْكَوَاكِبِ الْعُلْوِيَّةِ أَوْ قُبَّةٌ مِنَ الذَّهَبِ مَبْنِيَّةٌ أَوْ عَرُوسَةٌ مُجَلِّيَةٌ أَوْ لِيَّةٌ عَرَبِيَّةٌ كَمَا قَالَ فِيهَا الشَّاعِرُ حَيْثُ قَالَ —
sentences.tr: wa-hiya ka'annahā baʿḍu al-kawākibi al-ʿulwiyyati aw qubbatun mina al-dhahabi mabniyyatun aw ʿarūsatun mujalliyatun aw liyyatun ʿarabiyyatun kamā qāla fīhā al-shāʿiru ḥaythu qāla —
sentences.l: and she was as though she were one of the celestial stars, or a dome of gold, built, or a bride displayed [at her unveiling], or an Arabian... [obscure], as the poet said of her, when he said —
sentences.i: she seemed as though she were one of the stars on high, or a dome built of gold, or a bride displayed in her wedding finery, or [an obscure phrase] — as the poet said of her —
sentences.n: لية عربية is obscure and possibly corrupt: لية is not a recognizable noun continuing this list of similes (star / gold dome / bride), and may stand for some other word; it is left exactly as printed rather than guessed into shape.

sentences.t:
كانّها تبسّمَ عَنْ لولوٍ * أَوْ بردٍ أَوْ اقاحِ
وَ طرّةٍ كالليلِ مسبولةٍ * وَ بهجةٍ تخجلُ ضوءَ الصباحِ
sentences.tr:
kaʾannahā tabassama ʿan lūluwin * aw baradin aw uqāḥin
wa ṭurratin ka-al-layli masbūlatin * wa bahjatin tukhjilu ḍawʾa al-ṣabāḥi
sentences.l:
As though she, in smiling, revealed pearls, * or hailstones, or camomile-flowers,
and a forelock like the night let down, * and a radiance that puts to shame the light of morning.
sentences.i:
As if, when she smiled, she showed forth pearls, or hailstones, or white camomile-blossoms,
and a fringe of hair like night let loose, and a radiance before which the light of morning itself would blush.
sentences.n: بَرَد ('hail') and أُقَاح (a white camomile-like flower) are both stock images for white teeth. لولو is printed without its expected hamza-seat (لؤلؤ, 'pearl'); كانّها likewise lacks the hamza of كأنّها ('as though she'), the shadda alone carrying the doubled consonant — both are kept exactly as printed, being already-marked verse words.

sentences.t: قَٰلَ فَنَهَضَتِ الصَّبِيَّةُ الثَّالِثَةُ مِنْ فَوْقِ السَّرِيرِ وَ خَطَرَتْ مَهْلًا إِلَى أَنْ صَارَتْ فِي وَسَطِ الْقَاعَةِ عِنْدَ أَخَوَاتِهَا وَ قَالَتْ مَا وُقُوفُكُمْ حُطُّوا عَنْ رَأْسِ هَٰذَا الْمِسْكِينِ الْحَمَّالِ
sentences.tr: qāla fa-nahaḍati al-ṣabiyyatu al-thālithatu min fawqi al-sarīri wa-khaṭarat mahlan ilā an ṣārat fī wasaṭi al-qāʿati ʿinda akhawātihā wa-qālat mā wuqūfukum ḥuṭṭū ʿan ra'si hādhā al-miskīni al-ḥammāli
sentences.l: He said: Then the third girl rose up from atop the couch, and walked with a slow, swaying gait, until she came to be in the middle of the hall, by her sisters, and said, 'What [is] your standing [for]? Take [the load] down from the head of this poor porter.'
sentences.i: He said: Then the third girl rose from the couch and came forward with a slow, swaying grace, until she stood in the middle of the hall among her sisters, and said, 'Why are you standing there? Take the load down from this poor porter's head.'

sentences.t: فَجَاءَتِ الْخُوشْكَاشَةُ مِنْ قُدَّامُ وَالْبَوَّابَةُ مِنْ خَلْفُ وَسَاعَدَتْهُمُ الثَّالِثَةُ وَحَطُّوا الْقَفَصَ عَنِ الْحَمَّالِ وَأَفْرَغُوا مَا فِي الْقَفَصِ وَوَضَعُوا كُلَّ شَيْءٍ فِي مَحَلِّهِ وَأَعْطَوُا الْحَمَّالَ دِينَارَيْنِ وَقَالُوا لَهُ تَوَجَّهْ يَا حَمَّالُ
sentences.tr: fa-jā'ati al-khūshkāshatu min quddāmu wa-al-bawwābatu min khalfu wa-sāʿadathumu al-thālithatu wa-ḥaṭṭū al-qafaṣa ʿani al-ḥammāli wa-afraghū mā fī al-qafaṣi wa-waḍaʿū kulla shay'in fī maḥallihi wa-aʿṭawu al-ḥammāla dīnārayni wa-qālū lahu tawajjah yā ḥammālu
sentences.l: Then the marketing-girl came from in front, and the doorkeeper from behind, and the third one helped them, and they took the basket down from the porter, and emptied out what was in the basket, and put every thing in its place, and gave the porter two dinars, and said to him, 'Be off, O porter.'
sentences.i: So the marketing-girl came up in front and the doorkeeper from behind, and the third sister helped them, and they took the basket down from the porter, emptied out what was in it, put everything back in its place, gave the porter two dinars, and told him, 'Be on your way, porter.'
sentences.n: Here the marketing-girl's name is spelled الخوشكاشة rather than الشوشكاشة as earlier — the same character; the edition's spelling of this servant-title varies.

sentences.t: فَنَظَرَ إِلَى الصَّبَايَا وَمَا هُمْ فِيهِ مِنَ الْحُسْنِ وَالطَّبَايِعِ الْحِسَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-naẓara ilā al-ṣabāyā wa-mā hum fīhi mina al-ḥusni wa-al-ṭabāyiʿi al-ḥisāni
sentences.l: Then he looked at the girls and what they were in, of beauty and fair natures,
sentences.i: Then he looked at the girls, and their beauty and lovely natures,

sentences.t: فَمَا نَظَرَ أَحْسَنَ مِنْهُمْ وَمَا عِنْدَهُمْ رِجَالٌ
sentences.tr: fa-mā naẓara aḥsana minhum wa-mā ʿindahum rijālun
sentences.l: and he had not seen [any] more beautiful than them, and there was no men with them,
sentences.i: he had never seen any more beautiful, and there was not a man among them,

sentences.t: وَنَظَرَ مَا عِنْدَهُمْ مِنَ الشَّرَابِ وَالْفَوَاكِهِ وَالْمَشْمُومَاتِ وَغَيْرِ ذَٰلِكَ
sentences.tr: wa-naẓara mā ʿindahum mina al-sharābi wa-al-fawākihi wa-al-mashmūmāti wa-ghayri dhālika
sentences.l: and he saw what they had of drink, and fruits, and sweet-smelling things, and other than that,
sentences.i: and he saw the wine, the fruit, the sweet-scented herbs, and all else they had,

sentences.t: فَتَعَجَّبَ غَايَةَ الْعَجَبِ وَ تَوَقَّفَ عَنِ الْخُرُوجِ
sentences.tr: fa-taʿajjaba ghāyata al-ʿajabi wa-tawaqqafa ʿani al-khurūji
sentences.l: and he marveled the utmost marveling, and held back from going out,
sentences.i: so he marveled exceedingly, and lingered, unwilling to leave,

sentences.t: فَقَانَتْ لَهُ الصَّبِيَّةُ مَا لَكَ لِمَ لَا تَرُوحُ أَنْتَ كَأَنَّكَ اِسْتَقْلَيْتَ الْأُجْرَةَ
sentences.tr: fa-qānat lahu al-ṣabiyyatu mā laka lima lā tarūḥu anta ka'annaka istaqlayta al-ujrata
sentences.l: Then the girl [said] to him, 'What is [wrong] with you? Why do you not go? You, [it is] as though you have found the wage too little.'
sentences.i: Then the girl said to him, 'What's the matter with you? Why don't you go? It is as if you find the fee too small.'
sentences.n: فقانت is almost certainly a compositor's slip for فقالت ('she said'), a single letter off; it is kept exactly as printed. استقليت is a Middle-Arabic spelling of Classical استقللت ('you deemed [it] too little'), writing the doubled consonant of the root ق-ل-ل with a glide instead of a shadda; the same spelling recurs in the porter's reply below.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ اِلْتَفَتَتْ إِلَى أُخْتِهَا وَقَالَتْ لَهَا أَعْطِيهِ دِينَارًا آخَرَ
sentences.tr: thumma iltafatat ilā ukhtihā wa-qālat lahā aʿṭīhi dīnāran ākhara
sentences.l: Then she turned to her sister and said to her, 'Give him another dinar.'
sentences.i: Then she turned to her sister and said, 'Give him one more dinar.'

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْحَمَّالُ وَاللَّهِ يَا سِتِّي مَا اِسْتَقْلَيْتُ الْأُجْرَةَ وَأُجْرَتِي مَا تُسَاوِي دِرْهَمَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-ḥammālu wa-allāhi yā sittī mā istaqlaytu al-ujrata wa-ujratī mā tusāwī dirhamayni
sentences.l: The porter said, 'By God, my lady, I have not found the wage too little, and my wage is not worth two dirhams,
sentences.i: The porter said, 'By God, my lady, I do not think the fee too small — my wage is not worth even two dirhams,
sentences.n: سِتِّي ('my lady') is the colloquial form of the Classical سَيِّدَتِي.

sentences.t: وَإِنَّمَا اِشْتَغَلَ قَلْبِي وَسِرِّي بِكُمْ وَكَيْفَ أَنْتُمْ وَحْدَكُمْ مَا عِنْدَكُمْ رِجَالٌ وَلَا أَحَدٌ يُونِسُكُمْ
sentences.tr: wa-innamā ishtaghala qalbī wa-sirrī bikum wa-kayfa antum waḥdakum mā ʿindakum rijālun wa-lā aḥadun yūnisukum
sentences.l: but rather my heart and my inmost secret became occupied with you: how [is it that] you are alone, you have no men, and no one keeps you company,
sentences.i: but my heart and my very soul are taken up with you — how is it that you are here alone, with no men among you and no one to keep you company,
sentences.n: يونسكم is printed without the hamza-seat expected in Classical يؤنسكم ('gives you company'); kept as printed.

sentences.t: وَأَنْتُمْ تَعْرِفُونَ أَنَّ الْمَأْدُبَةَ لَا تَقِفُ إِلَّا عَلَى أَرْبَعَةٍ وَمَا لَكُمْ رَابِعٌ وَمَا يَطِيبُ لَعِبُ النِّسَاءِ إِلَّا بِالرِّجَالِ
sentences.tr: wa-antum taʿrifūna anna al-ma'dubata lā taqifu illā ʿalā arbaʿatin wa-mā lakum rābiʿun wa-mā yaṭību laʿibu al-nisā'i illā bi-al-rijāli
sentences.l: and you [yourselves] know that the banquet does not stand except upon four, and you have no fourth, and the play of women is not sweet except with men.'
sentences.i: and you yourselves know that a feast is not complete except with four, and you lack a fourth — and women's merrymaking is only sweet with men.'
sentences.n: The porter alludes to a proverb that a proper convivial gathering rests on four participants, as a table rests on four legs; the sisters, being three, lack the fourth.

sentences.t: كَمَا قِيلَ شِعْرٌ قِيلَ شِعْرٌ
sentences.tr: kamā qīla shiʿrun qīla shiʿrun
sentences.l: as was said — verse; [it] was said — verse:
sentences.i: — as it is said, in verse; it is said, in verse:
sentences.n: قيل شعر is the edition's own editorial marker announcing that a poem follows; it appears twice here, apparently a printer's duplication. The verse it introduces falls outside this excerpt.

sentences.t:
أَما تَرَى أَربَعاً لِلَّهوِ قَل جَمَعَت * جَنكٌ وَ عُودٌ وَ قَانُونٌ وَ مِزمَارُ
وَ وَافَقَتها مِنَ المَشمُومِ اَربَعَة * وَردٌ وَ آسٌ وَ مَنشُورٌ وَ نُوّارُ
وَ لَيسَ يَحسُنُ ذَا الَّا بِاَربَعَة * خَمرٌ وَ رَوضٌ وَ مَعشُوقٌ وَ دِينَارُ
sentences.tr:
amā tarā arbaʿan lil-lahwi qal jamaʿat * jankun wa ʿūdun wa qānūnun wa mizmāru
wa wāfaqathā mina al-mashmūmi arbaʿah * wardun wa āsun wa manshūrun wa nuwwāru
wa laysa yaḥsunu dhā illā bi-arbaʿah * khamrun wa rawḍun wa maʿshūqun wa dīnāru
sentences.l:
Do you not see four things for pleasure that rarely came together * a harp, and a lute, and a qanun, and a flute?
And matching them, of things smelled, four * a rose, and myrtle, and a manshūr-flower, and blossoms.
And this is not made fair except by four * wine, and a garden, and a beloved, and a gold coin.
sentences.i:
Do you ever see four things for pleasure come together? Rarely — the harp, the lute, the qanun, and the flute.
And matching them, four fragrances: the rose, the myrtle, the manshūr-blossom, and the flowering spray.
Yet none of it is truly lovely without four things more: wine, a garden, a beloved, and gold.
sentences.n: The edition prints قَل without a shadda where the sense is qalla, 'rarely'; kept as printed. منشور (manshūr, lit. 'unfolded') is an unusual spelling for a fragrant flower, perhaps a variant of منثور, narcissus or scattered blossom; kept as printed.

sentences.t: وَأَنْتُمْ ثَلٰثَةٌ وَتَحْتَاجُونَ إِلَى رَابِعٍ وَيَكُونُ رَجُلًا عَاقِلًا لَبِيبًا حَاذِقًا وَ لِلْأَسْرَارِ كَاتِمًا
sentences.tr: wa-antum thalāthatun wa-taḥtājūna ilā rābiʿin wa-yakūnu rajulan ʿāqilan labīban ḥādhiqan wa-lil-asrāri kātiman
sentences.l: And you are three, and you need a fourth, and he should be a sensible man, intelligent, skillful, and a keeper of secrets.
sentences.i: And you are three, and you need a fourth — a man who is sensible, sharp-witted and shrewd, and who can keep a secret.
sentences.n: ثَلٰثَةٌ is printed defectively (ثلثة, without the medial alif); pointed here with a dagger alif to preserve the rasm. The porter addresses the three women with the masculine plural antum, a loose, unmarked form of address typical of this text's Middle Arabic rather than a grammatical slip.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعُوا كَلَامَهُ أَعْجَبَهُمْ وَضَحِكُوا عَلَيْهِ وَقَالُوا وَمَنْ لَنَا بِذَلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿū kalāmahu aʿjabahum wa-ḍaḥikū ʿalayhi wa-qālū wa-man lanā bi-dhālika
sentences.l: Then when they heard his words, it pleased them, and they laughed at him, and they said, 'And who for us with that?'
sentences.i: When they heard what he said, they were delighted, and they laughed at him, and said, 'But who will vouch to us for that?'
sentences.n: 'man lanā bi-dhālika', literally 'who is there for us with that', is an idiom for demanding a guarantee: 'who will answer for it?'

sentences.t: وَنَحْنُ بَنَاتٌ نَخَافُ نُودِعَ السِّرَّ لِمَنْ لَا يَحْفَظُهُ وَقَدْ قَرَأْنَا فِي بَعْضِ الْأَخْبَارِ مَا قَالَهُ ابْنُ الثَّمَّامِ شِعْرٌ فِي بَعْضِ الْأَخْبَارِ مَا قَالَهُ ابْنُ الثَّمَّامِ شِعْرٌ
sentences.tr: wa-naḥnu banātun nakhāfu nūdiʿa al-sirra li-man lā yaḥfaẓuhu wa-qad qaraʾnā fī baʿḍi al-akhbāri mā qālahu ibnu al-thammāmi shiʿrun fī baʿḍi al-akhbāri mā qālahu ibnu al-thammāmi shiʿrun
sentences.l: And we are girls; we fear to entrust the secret to whoever does not keep it. And we have read, in some of the reports, what Ibn al-Thammām said — verse — in some of the reports, what Ibn al-Thammām said — verse:
sentences.i: And we are only girls; we are afraid of trusting a secret to someone who will not keep it. And we have read, in a certain account, what Ibn al-Thammām said — some verses:
sentences.n: The edition prints the whole clause 'in some of the reports, what Ibn al-Thammām said — verse' twice in a row, evidently a compositor's slip in resetting the line; reproduced here exactly as printed.

sentences.t:
صُنِ السِّرَّ جَهلَك وَلا تُودِعهُ * فَمَن اَودَعَ السِّرَّ قَد ضَيَّعَه
مَنْ أَطْلَعَ النَّاسَ عَلَى سِرِّهِ * اسْتَوْجَبَ الذُّلَّ فِي جَبْهَتِهِ
sentences.tr:
ṣuni al-sirra jahlaka wa-lā tūdiʿhu * fa-man awdaʿa al-sirra qad ḍayyaʿah
man aṭlaʿa al-nāsa ʿalā sirrihi * istawjaba al-dhulla fī jabhatihi
sentences.l:
Guard the secret [with] your ignorance, and do not entrust it * for whoever entrusts the secret has indeed lost it.
Whoever lets people learn of his secret * has earned disgrace upon his brow.
sentences.i:
Guard your secret with all your might, and confide it to no one — for whoever confides a secret has already thrown it away.
Whoever lets others learn his secret has earned open shame.
sentences.n: The edition prints جَهلَك, 'your ignorance', where the sense ('guard it with your utmost effort') calls for جُهْدَك, 'your utmost'; kept exactly as printed, a likely compositor's slip.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْحَمَّالُ فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ كَلَامَهُمْ وَحَيَائَهُمْ إِنِّي رَجُلٌ عَاقِلٌ أَمِينٌ قَرَأْتُ الْكُتُبَ وَطَالَعْتُ التَّوَارِيخَ أَظْهَرْتُ الْجَمِيلَ وَأَخْفَيْتُ الْقَبِيحَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-ḥammālu fa-lammā samiʿa kalāmahum wa-ḥayāʾahum innī rajulun ʿāqilun amīnun qaraʾtu al-kutuba wa-ṭālaʿtu al-tawārīkha aẓhartu al-jamīla wa-akhfaytu al-qabīḥa
sentences.l: The porter said — when he heard their words and their modesty — 'I am indeed a sensible, trustworthy man; I have read books and studied histories; I have shown the fair and hidden the foul.'
sentences.i: The porter, hearing their words and their modesty, said, 'I am indeed a sensible and trustworthy man. I have read books and studied histories; I have shown what is fair and concealed what is foul.'
sentences.n: The clause order here ('the porter said... when he heard...') puts the 'when'-clause after the main verb rather than before it, a looseness typical of this text's syntax; translated for sense.

sentences.t: وَالشَّاعِرُ يَقُولُ فِي كَلَامِهِ وَأَنْشَدَ
sentences.tr: wa-al-shāʿiru yaqūlu fī kalāmihi wa-anshada
sentences.l: And the poet says, in his words — and he recited:
sentences.i: As the poet says — and he recited:

sentences.t:
مَا يَكْتُمُ السِّرَّ الَّا كُلُّ ذِي ثِقَةٍ * وَالسِّرُّ عِنْدَ خِيَارِ النَّاسِ مَكْتُومُ
السِّرُّ عِنْدِي فِي بَيْتٍ لَهُ غَلَقٌ * ضَاعَتْ مَفَاتِيحُهُ وَالْبَابُ مَخْتُومُ
sentences.tr:
mā yaktumu al-sirra illā kullu dhī thiqatin * wa-al-sirru ʿinda khiyāri al-nāsi maktūmu
al-sirru ʿindī fī baytin lahu ghalaqun * ḍāʿat mafātīḥuhu wa-al-bābu makhtūmu
sentences.l:
None keeps the secret except every possessor of trustworthiness * and the secret, with the best of people, is kept.
The secret, with me, is in a house that has a lock * its keys are lost, and the door is sealed.
sentences.i:
No one keeps a secret but a man of proven trust — with the best of people, a secret stays kept.
My secret is locked in a house whose keys are lost, and whose door is sealed shut.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعُوا الْبَنَاتُ الشِّعْرَ وَالنِّظَامَ وَمَا أَبَاحَ قُلْنَ لَهُ أَنْتَ تَعْلَمُ أَنَّنَا غَرِمْنَا عَلَى هَٰذَا الْمَقَامِ جُمْلَةً
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿū al-banātu al-shiʿra wa-al-niẓāma wa-mā abāḥa qulna lahu anta taʿlamu annanā gharimnā ʿalā hādhā al-maqāmi jumlatan
sentences.l: Then when the girls heard the verse and the rhyme and what it disclosed, they said to him, 'You know that we have spent, on this occasion, a sum —
sentences.i: When the girls heard the verse, its rhyme, and what it revealed, they said to him, 'You know we have laid out a good sum —

sentences.t: مِنَ الْمَالِ فَهَلْ مَعَكَ شَيْءٌ تَعَارَفْنَا بِهِ فَنَحْنُ مَا نَدَعُكَ تَجْلِسُ عِنْدَنَا وَتَصِيرُ نَدِيمَنَا وَتُشْرِفُ عَلَى وُجُوهَنَا الصِّبَاحَ الْمِلَاحَ حَتَّى تُوزَنَ جُمْلَةٌ مِنَ الْمَالِ
sentences.tr: mina al-māli fa-hal maʿaka shayʾun taʿārafnā bihi fa-naḥnu mā nadaʿuka tajlisu ʿindanā wa-taṣīru nadīmanā wa-tushrifu ʿalā wujūhanā al-ṣibāḥa al-milāḥa ḥattā tūzana jumlatun mina al-māli
sentences.l: — of money. So do you have something by which we become acquainted with each other? For we will not leave you [to] sit with us, and become our boon-companion, and gaze upon our fair, lovely faces, until a sum of money is weighed out.
sentences.i: — of money on this gathering. So do you have something to offer, to seal our acquaintance? For we will not let you sit with us, become our companion, and feast your eyes on our fair, lovely faces — not until a sum of money has been weighed out.
sentences.n: الصباح الملاح is read here as a rhyming pair of adjectives, 'fair and lovely' (plurals of ṣabīḥ and malīḥ), describing the faces, rather than as 'fine mornings' — matching the passage's rhymed prose.

sentences.t: أَلَا مَا سَمِعْتَ صَاحِبَ الْمَثَلِ وَقُلْ قَالَ مَحَبَّةٌ بِلَا حَبَّهٍ مَا تُسَاوِي حَبَّهً
sentences.tr: alā mā samiʿta ṣāḥiba al-mathali wa-qul qāla muḥabbatun bilā ḥabbahin mā tusāwī ḥabbahan
sentences.l: Now, have you not heard the master of the proverb — and say: he said, 'Affection without a grain is not worth a grain.'
sentences.i: Now, have you not heard the proverb-maker's saying? Say it: he said, 'Love without a grain to it isn't worth a grain.'
sentences.n: This clause is compressed in the edition; أَلَا is read here as the attention-calling particle ('now then') and وَقُلْ as a literal imperative, 'say', introducing the quoted proverb, rather than as a spelling of some other word. The saying puns on حَبَّة (a grain, a seed) echoing حُبّ/مَحَبَّة (love): affection with nothing behind it is worth nothing.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتِ الْبَوَّابَةُ مَعَكَ شَيْءٌ يَا حَبِيبِي
sentences.tr: fa-qālati al-bawwābatu maʿaka shayʾun yā ḥabībī
sentences.l: Then the doorkeeper said, 'Do you have something, my darling?'
sentences.i: Then the doorkeeper-girl said, 'Have you got anything, my love?'
sentences.n: 'The doorkeeper' (al-bawwābah) is one of the three sisters, named here by her role in the house.

sentences.t: أَنْتَ شَيْءٌ مَا مَعَكَ شَيْءٌ رُوحْ بِلَا شَيْءٍ
sentences.tr: anta shayʾun mā maʿaka shayʾun rūḥ bilā shayʾin
sentences.l: You are a thing! You have not a thing! Go, without a thing!
sentences.i: You're something, all right — but you haven't got a thing on you! Off with you, empty-handed!
sentences.n: رُوحْ, 'go!', is spelled with a full wāw, the colloquial imperative still used in spoken Egyptian Arabic, rather than the Classical رُحْ; kept as printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتِ الْخَوْشْكَاشَةُ يَا إِخْوَتِي كُفُّوا عَنْهُ فَوَاللَّهِ مَا قَصَّرَ الْيَوْمَ مَعَنَا وَلَوْ كَانَ غَيْرَهُ مَا طَوَّلَ رُوحَهُ مَعَنَا وَ مَهْمَا جَاءَ عَلَيْهِ أَنَا أُوزِنُهُ عَنْهُ
sentences.tr: fa-qālati al-khawshkāshatu yā ikhwatī kuffū ʿanhu fa-wallāhi mā qaṣṣara al-yawma maʿanā wa-law kāna ghayrahu mā ṭawwala rūḥahu maʿanā wa-mahmā jāʾa ʿalayhi anā ūzinuhu ʿanhu
sentences.l: Then the marketing-girl said, 'O my sisters, leave off him — for by God, he has not fallen short with us today; and had it been another, he would not have prolonged his stay with us; and whatever falls due upon him, I will weigh it out for him.'
sentences.i: Then the marketing-girl said, 'Sisters, let him be — by God, he hasn't stinted with us today, and had it been anyone else, he would not have lasted this long in our company. Whatever he owes, I'll pay it myself.'
sentences.n: الخوشكاشة (spelled variously across this night: الشوشكاشة، الخوشكاشة، الخشكاشة) is the household marketing-girl, one of the three sisters, named by her role rather than a personal name — the same servant-title as at sentence 74/83, with the edition's spelling of it varying. روحه ('his rūḥ', his soul) is used idiomatically for 'himself'.

sentences.t: فَفَرِحَ الْحَمَّالُ وَقَبَّلَ الْأَرْضَ وَشَكَرَ فَقَالَتْ صَاحِبَةُ السَّرِيرِ وَاللَّهِ مَا نَدَعُكَ تَجْلِسُ عِنْدَنَا إِلَّا بِشَرْطٍ
sentences.tr: fa-fariḥa al-ḥammālu wa-qabbala al-arḍa wa-shakara fa-qālat ṣāḥibatu al-sarīri wallāhi mā nadaʿuka tajlisu ʿindanā illā bi-sharṭin
sentences.l: So the porter rejoiced, and kissed the ground, and gave thanks. Then the mistress of the couch said, 'By God, we will not leave you [to] sit with us except on a condition —'
sentences.i: The porter was overjoyed; he kissed the ground and gave thanks. Then the mistress of the couch said, 'By God, we will let you stay with us on one condition only —'
sentences.n: 'The mistress of the couch' (ṣāḥibat al-sarīr) is another of the three sisters, again named by her role.

sentences.t: وَهُوَ أَنْ لَا يَسْأَلَ عَمَّا لَا يَعْنِيهِ وَإِنْ تَفَاضَلَ يُضْرَبْ فَقَالَ الْحَمَّالُ رَضِيتُ يَا سِتِّي عَلَى الرَّأْسِ وَالْعَيْنِ وَهَا أَنَا بِلَا لِسَانٍ
sentences.tr: wa-huwa an lā yasʾala ʿammā lā yaʿnīhi wa-in tafāḍala yuḍrab fa-qāla al-ḥammālu raḍītu yā sittī ʿalā al-raʾsi wa-al-ʿayni wa-hā anā bilā lisānin
sentences.l: '— which is that he not ask about what does not concern him, and if he oversteps, he is beaten.' The porter said, 'I agree, my lady — upon the head and the eye, and here I am without a tongue.'
sentences.i: '— that he not pry into what is none of his business, and if he oversteps, he will be beaten.' The porter said, 'Agreed, my lady — gladly, with all my heart, and here I am as good as mute.'
sentences.n: تَفَاضَلَ is an unusual verb form here; the context calls for something like 'oversteps, presumes', which is how it is rendered, though the reading is not certain. 'Upon the head and the eye' (ʿalā al-raʾsi wa-al-ʿayni) is a common idiom of wholehearted consent, distinct from the stock phrase 'with hearing and obedience'.

sentences.t: فَقَامَتِ الْخَوْشْكَاشَةُ وَشَدَّتْ وَسَطَهَا وَصَفَّتِ الْقَنَانِيَ وَرَوَّقَتِ الْمُدَامَ وَعَمِلَتِ الْخُضْرَةَ عَلَى جَانِبٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qāmati al-khawshkāshatu wa-shaddat wasaṭahā wa-ṣaffati al-qanāniya wa-rawwaqati al-mudāma wa-ʿamilati al-khuḍrata ʿalā jānibin
sentences.l: Then the marketing-girl rose, and bound her waist, and lined up the flasks, and strained the wine, and set the greens on one side —
sentences.i: The marketing-girl then rose, tied up her waist, set out the flasks, strained the wine, and laid out the relish to one side —

sentences.t: الْجَرَّةَ وَ أَحْضَرَتْ مَا يَحْتَاجُونَ إِلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: al-jarrata wa-aḥḍarat mā yaḥtājūna ilayhi
sentences.l: ...the jar. And she brought what they needed.
sentences.i: ...the jar, and brought whatever they might need.
sentences.n: This line opens mid-sentence: it completes a list of vessels begun on the line before this excerpt, so 'the jar' has no verb of its own here.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَدَّمَتِ الْمُدَامَ وَ جَلَسَتْ هِيَ وَ أُخْتَاهَا وَ جَلَسَ الْحَمَّالُ بَيْنَهُنَّ وَ هُوَ يَظُنُّ أَنَّهُ فِي الْمَنَامِ
sentences.tr: thumma qaddamati al-mudāma wa-jalasat hiya wa-ukhtāhā wa-jalasa al-ḥammālu baynahunna wa-huwa yaẓunnu annahu fī al-manāmi
sentences.l: Then she served the wine, and she and her two sisters sat down, and the porter sat among them while he thought that he was in a dream.
sentences.i: Then she brought out the wine, and she and her two sisters sat down, and the porter sat among them, thinking himself in a dream.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَدَّمَتْ بَاطِيَةَ الْمُدَامِ وَ مَلَأَتْ أَوَّلَ قَدَحٍ وَ شَرِبَتْهُ وَ الثَّانِيَ وَ الثَّالِثَ
sentences.tr: thumma qaddamat bāṭiyata al-mudāmi wa-malaʾat awwala qadaḥin wa-sharibathu wa-al-thāniya wa-al-thālitha
sentences.l: Then she brought the flagon of wine, and filled a first cup and drank it, and the second and the third.
sentences.i: Then she brought out the flagon of wine, filled a first cup and drained it, then the second, then the third.
sentences.n: The mistress of the house drinks three cups herself before the round is passed on to the others.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ مَلَأَتْ وَ نَاوَلَتْ أُخْتَهَا الْأُخْرَى
sentences.tr: thumma malaʾat wa-nāwalat ukhtahā al-ukhrā
sentences.l: Then she filled [a cup] and handed it to her other sister.
sentences.i: Then she filled another cup and passed it to her other sister.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ مَلَأَتْ وَ نَاوَلَتِ الْحَمَّالَ وَ قَالَتْ
sentences.tr: thumma malaʾat wa-nāwalati al-ḥammāla wa-qālat
sentences.l: Then she filled [a cup] and handed it to the porter, and said:
sentences.i: Then she filled a cup, handed it to the porter, and said:

sentences.t: اِشْرَبْ هَنِيئاً مُتَّسِعاً بِالْعَوافِي * اِنَّ هَذَا الشُّرْبَ لِلدَّاءِ شَافِي
sentences.tr: ishrab hanīʾan muttasiʿan bi-al-ʿawāfī * inna hādhā al-shurba li-al-dāʾi shāfī
sentences.l: Drink, wholesome and abundant, in good health * indeed this drink is a cure for illness.
sentences.i: Drink, and may it bring you ease and health unstinted * for indeed this draught is a cure for every ill.
sentences.n: A conventional toast offered along with the cup; the idea of wine as a physician's cure recurs through the verses that follow.

sentences.t: فَأَخَذَ الْكَأْسَ بِيَدِهِ وَ خَدَمَ وَ شَكَرَ وَ أَنْشَدَ يَقُولُ شِعْرٌ
sentences.tr: fa-akhadha al-kaʾsa bi-yadihi wa-khadama wa-shakara wa-anshada yaqūlu shiʿrun
sentences.l: So he took the cup in his hand, and paid homage, and gave thanks, and recited, saying, in verse:
sentences.i: So he took the cup in his hand, bowed in courtesy, gave thanks, and recited these lines:

sentences.t:
مَا تَشْرَبُ الْكَاسَ الَّا مَعَ اَخٍ ثِقَةٍ * وَ طَاهِرِ الْاَصْلِ مَنْسُوباً اِلَى السَّلَفِ
فَالرَّاحُ كَالرِّيحِ اِنْ هَبَّتْ عَلَى عِطْرٍ * طَابَتْ وَتَنْتُنْ اِنْ مَرَّتْ عَلَى الْجِيَفِ
sentences.tr:
mā tashrabu al-kāsa illā maʿa akhin thiqatin * wa-ṭāhiri al-aṣli mansūban ilā al-salafi
fa-al-rāḥu ka-al-rīḥi in habbat ʿalā ʿiṭrin * ṭābat wa-tantunu in marrat ʿalā al-jiyafi
sentences.l:
